planting.note: Divide and plant established clumps in spring once new growth begins; set into open, sunny ground that stays reliably moist through the growing season.

directions: This long-grown selection sends up tall, gently arching flower spikes that open green and purple before ripening to a golden brown and finally a clear butter yellow by autumn, giving the clump a slow color shift that lasts for months. Grow it in open, sunny ground that ranges from average to consistently damp, since it colors and stands best where moisture never runs short in summer. The narrow basal foliage stays low and tidy while the towering stems do the visual work, so place it where its height and late-season glow can be appreciated against a dark background. Cut the whole clump back hard to the ground in late winter before new shoots emerge.

planting.note: Set divisions in spring into open, sunny beds; it tolerates both drier soils and periodically wet ground better than most named selections.

directions: Overdam forms a strong mound of green foliage from which many fairly upright stems rise, carrying flowers that start a dusky purple and warm to orange and yellow tones as autumn arrives, on a notably shorter and more compact frame than most purple moor grass selections. It accepts a wider moisture range than many cultivars, handling both drier spells and heavier, damp soil without complaint, though full sun keeps the habit tightest. Its more modest height makes it useful in smaller borders or container groupings where taller selections like 'Skyracer' would overwhelm the space. Shear the dried stems close to the ground in late winter ahead of spring regrowth.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in open, sunny ground; its compact size suits smaller borders and mixed grass plantings better than the taller selections.

directions: Named for a Danish nurseryman, this compact selection forms dense clumps that stay noticeably smaller than most purple moor grass cultivars, sending up softly upright, initially purple flower stems that take on warm autumn tones later in the season. Grow it in open, sunny ground that tolerates both dry spells and periods of heavier, damp soil, since this cultivar is more forgiving of variable moisture than many relatives. Its modest scale makes it a natural fit near the front of a sunny border or worked through smaller drifts where larger moor grasses would crowd out neighbors. Cut the dried foliage and stems back close to the ground before new growth resumes in late winter.

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring into open, sunny ground kept evenly moist; set at higher density than taller selections since this cultivar runs smaller and tighter.

directions: Torch is a distinctly upright selection of purple moor grass, holding its flowering stems rigidly vertical above a tight basal clump of green foliage rather than arching outward the way many cultivars do. Autumn brings a noticeable color shift through the foliage and stems, and the strict vertical habit reads as a strong architectural accent even in a mixed border. Grow it in open sun in soil that ranges from average to reliably damp, planting at closer spacing than taller Molinia selections since the clumps stay relatively narrow. Cut the whole plant back to the base in late winter before new shoots appear.

planting.note: Set spring divisions into open, sunny ground with reliable moisture; give it room, since the tidy foliage mound sends up tall, airy stems well above the clump.

directions: Bergfreund builds a tidy mound of narrow green foliage topped by open, airy flower stems that stand well clear of the clump and turn vivid orange and yellow as the season closes, making it one of the showier tall selections for fall color. It prefers open sun and takes average to heavy, consistently wet soils better than most ornamental grasses, which suits it to rain gardens or low spots that stay damp. The see-through quality of the flower stems lets it be planted mid-border without blocking the view of plants behind it. Cut the entire clump down to the ground in late winter before new foliage emerges.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in sun or light shade; because clumps can decline after a few years, plan to divide and replant the most vigorous sections on a regular cycle.

directions: Mill End builds large, dark green mounds of foliage from which tall flower stems rise enthusiastically, producing one of the bigger-scale displays among tufted hair grass selections. Grow it in average to quite damp, humus-rich soil in full sun or light shade, where the dark foliage and towering stems both fade gradually to a soft beige as summer turns to fall. Because the clumps tend to be relatively short-lived compared with the species, lift and divide every few years to keep plantings vigorous rather than letting an aging center go hollow. Trim the spent stems and foliage back close to the ground in late winter before fresh growth starts.

planting.note: Plant spring divisions in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in sun or light shade; divide and replant periodically, since clumps of this older selection can lose vigor after several years.

directions: Goldgehänge, whose German name translates roughly to 'golden pendant,' is one of the longer-established tufted hair grass selections, producing drooping, delicately branched flower sprays that open purplish before shifting toward a soft gold over dark green clumps of foliage. Grow it in average to quite moist, humus-rich soil in full sun or light shade, conditions under which both the dangling flower heads and foliage eventually dry to a pale beige by late summer. The pendant habit of the flower heads gives it a softer, more relaxed presence than stiffly upright hair grass selections, useful for breaking up rigid plant forms nearby. Cut the whole clump back close to the ground in late winter before new shoots appear.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in sun or light shade; as with other named selections of this species, divide every few seasons to keep clumps from thinning out.

directions: A more recent European introduction, Cabana Buta builds mounds of dark green foliage topped in summer by large, billowing, cloud-like flower heads carried on relatively tall stems. Grow it in average to quite damp, humus-rich soil in full sun or light shade, where both the foliage and the airy flower clusters gradually fade to beige as the season advances toward fall. The denser, puffier texture of its flower heads gives it a softer, more voluminous look than wirier hair grass cultivars, making it effective as a textural foil for bold-leaved shade perennials. Because clumps can be relatively short-lived, divide and replant vigorous sections every few years to maintain a full-looking planting.
